doc.title: Jimmy Wormworth interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 6, 2002

title: Lou Donaldson's records and the wave of players arriving in New York
summary: Introduced to Donaldson through Torrie Zito's record collection; he recalls Wayne Shorter and Coltrane at jam sessions.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: Let me throw a couple names at you and see just your recollections. Lou Donaldson?

He was kind of a spiritual and artistic father to me. I met him the same way I met Charlie Rouse. Well first of all before I left home Torrie Zito was working in the strip joints and all that and writing arrangements for some of the acts in those strip joints in Rome and Utica, and made good money, and would buy up all of the latest Blue Note records and whatever, Verve records. He’d order them from New York, mostly because you couldn’t get them in Utica too much. And so I’d go to visit Ronnie and Ronnie and I would lie on the floor in front of the phonograph and listen to all these records. And that’s where I first heard Lou Donaldson. I guess that Thelonious Monk record where they play “Round About Midnight” and “Eronel” — which is Lenore spelled backwards. I’ve asked around, who’s Lenore. I think somebody knows. I think Larry Ridley knows or Charles Davis. So that was my introduction to Lou Donaldson. And needless to say he impressed me. I loved his playing. I guess he had come to New York not too long before that and was an instant hit and when those records “A Night At Birdland” with Art Blakey, Horace Silver, Lou and Clifford Brown came out, well I was just in love with — well the whole record, but Lou included. And I came to New York and Lou is one of those people who is always out. He totally lives the jazz life, playing, everything, socializing. And he was always out at the jam sessions. And it just so happened when I came to New York a whole wave of guys came to New York who ended up doing very well — Freddie Hubbard, Larry Ridley, oh so many, and guys who from around here — Wayne Shorter, who was just getting out of the Army at the time. I can remember him playing jam sessions in his Army uniform, his summer khakis , getting up on the bandstand and playing in his summer khakis. I can remember Coltrane being back in the corner just listening and smiling and while Wayne is breaking the whole place up with this outlandish stuff. Curiously enough, my daughter ended up working with Wayne doing a couple of tours with him with his fusion band. And well anyway, Lou was always there and I knew who
